NSFAS Corruption

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
While everyone is looking at what's happening in the student protests, we should also be looking at NSFAS - because a closer look reveals R7 billion in irregular expenditure.

Unique Selling Point:
Parliament’s portfolio committee on Higher Education, Science and Technology has described the National Students Financial Aid Scheme (NSFAS) audit outcomes under administration as the “worst ever”.
The latest NSFAS annual report has revealed irregular expenditure of R7.5 billion. Irregular expenditure is actually even higher, with the Auditor General saying that an additional R50bn in irregular expenditure 'should have been disclosed as a result of disbursements made against eligibility criteria and conditions that were set without consultations with the minister or eligibility criteria and conditions not gazetted'.

Part of the problem that has given rise to the irregular expenditure is that there has been syndicated fraud and corruption where "ghost students" have been getting paid without proper checks being done before payments are made. Irregular expenditure is not corruption per se - it means that the proper procedures required by legislation have not been followed.

The extent of corruption will be quantified when the amount lost due to 'material irregularity' - the Auditor General's new audit category that gives the AG teeth - is determined. However at the time of the audit, the amount lost due to material irregularity had not been determined by the NSFAS administrator, Randall Carolissen. It is clear that since his arrival as Administrator there are some new controls that have been put in place and cases of fraud have been handed over to law enforcement, whereas previously the irregular expenditure wasn't even being detected.

Summary:
NSFAS has R7.5 billion in irregular expenditure.
There is a further R50bn that the auditor general is concerned is irregular expenditure.
This is the third year in a row that NSFAS has a qualified audit (bad audit outcome).
Student protests come at the end of a chain of administrative actions that do not get performed timeously.
In essence the Fees Must Fall protests are budget advocacy and a financial issue.
If one reverses from the moment of Mthokozisi Ntumba's incredibly sad death, there has been a slow violence in the institutional failings at NSFAS.
It may not be immediately apparent that social justice can looks like administrative justice and everyday actions that public officials must take require exercising their mandate in alignment with the Constitution and the Public Finance Management Act.
The institution and its systems have been under enormous additional pressure since the 2015 fee free tertiary education announcement, as it would have suddenly needed to do a lot more than previously.
It has emerged that there has been syndicated fraud and corruption. One of the types of fraud that have been discovered is that there have been ghost students who have been paid, because NSFAS wasn't doing enough to ensure that the students who were approved were indeed eligible to receive the funding. There are thousands of records of this nature, where students were approved without the correct documentation and checks being done. Only 40% of these records had been checked by the time the latest audit report was completed.
To eradicate this syndicated fraud requires proper IT systems, good internal controls, integrity by those in key positions at NSFAS.
A number of criminal complaints have been referred to the Special Investigating Unit to investigate. Parliament's Standing Committee on Public Accounts is frustrated with the pace of addressing these issues at NSFAS.

ABOUT NSFAS
NSFAS = National Student Financial Aid Scheme
NSFAS was established according to the National Student Financial Aid Scheme Act (Act 56 of 1999) and incorporated TEFSA (Tertiary Education Fund of South Africa). From 1993 to 2000, TEFSA was the primary non-profit company in terms of Section 21 of the Companies Act and ceased to operate in July 2000. All existing loans on the TEFSA books were transferred to NSFAS.
It is a public entity under the Department of Higher Education and Training (DHET). NSFAS is managed, governed and administered by the NSFAS Board, with the Minister of Higher Education and Training as the Executive Authority.
NSFAS is currently under administration. It was placed under administration in August 2018. This was after increasing audit evidence of maladministration, as well as delays of up to eight months in funding of the majority of students.
For more information: https://www.nsfas.org.za/content/governance.html

WHAT DOES NSFAS DO?
NSFAS provides financial assistance in the form of loans or bursaries to eligible students at public higher education institutions and Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) colleges. It administers loans and bursaries, and recovers the loans from the students once they are employed and earning in excess of R30,000 per annum.
Following the announcement of the new bursary funding programme by the former President of South Africa in December 2017, financial assistance to all eligible students is now in the form of bursaries from the 2018 academic year.
The new bursary scheme introduced a new set of criteria to expand the reach of NSFAS funding as well as promote throughput of students. The household income threshold was raised from R122 000 to R350 000 per annum for First-Time Entering Students (FTENs) in 2018 onwards, and a new qualification criterion of R600 000 per annum household income threshold for students with a disability was introduced.
This leaves the 'missing middle' as a student issue, because it's hard for households earning just above R350,000 per annum and upwards as well to afford to send their children to get a tertiary education.

Press Release:


NSFAS in Shambles

When former president Jacob Zuma said education would be free for students from low-income families, no one knew where the money would come from – the National Student Financial Aid Scheme (NSFAS) would have to overcome that challenge. Now, six years later, what little funds were found have been mismanaged because of a lack of accountability and management systems. This has led to R7-billion worth of irregular expenditure, corruption allegations and several investigations with the latest finding showing some funds have gone to "ghost students". As NSFAS counts the cost of its third bad audit outcome in a row, Carte Blanche investigates what it means for students who suffer the consequences when bursaries come late – or never.

Producer: Sasha Schwendenwein | Presenter: Claire Mawisa

Script:


IT’S ALMOST BECOME AN ANNUAL RITUAL FOR STUDENTS TO PROTEST FOR THE RIGHT TO EDUCATION …AND FOR THE PROTEST TO BE MET WITH POLICE BRUTALITY AND VIOLENCE. BUT HERE’S WHAT BEING BROKE MEANS: POOR STUDENTS WHO CANNOT AFFORD TO BETTER THEMSELVES VERSUS AN EDUCATION SYSTEM THAT SAYS WE CANNOT AFFORD TO MAKE IT FREE. BUT WHAT NO ONE IS ASKING: IS GOVERNMENT MANAGING WHAT LITTLE FUNDS WE HAVE CORRECTLY?

In 2015 Wits student Shaeera Kalla was shot 13 times with rubber bullets… but it’s 2021 and the FeesMustFall protests have continued as a symptom of the institutional failings of our government to fund its free education promise through the National Student Financial Aid Scheme or NSFAS.

Shaeera: when the free education announcement was made by President Jacob Zuma, there was no indication of where the money was coming from.

Kalla, a former student activist, feels the government hasn't found a solution to that conundrum.

C: So then how does it feel for you personally when you see that the student protests are happening in 2021 for I could say exactly the same reasons?

It's a very frustrating and disillusioning, you're not seeing any real change in these systems. NSFAS was still being seen as part of the solution, when in fact it was part of the problem.

NSFAS falls under the department of higher education and training, and has existed since 1999, primarily offering student loans. But in 2015, it underwent a facelift almost overnight; and now it is 100% focused on giving bursaries. These NSFAS marketing videos explain what a student can now expect…

Upsound: we get XYZ

All a student needs in order to apply is a university acceptance and an annual household income less than R350,000.

C: Has that not helped students?

K: Fundamentally, we cannot say that NSFAS has become a competent institution that can administer the funds that have been put into it.

Over the past 6 years NSFAS has been rocked by allegations of corruption and embezzlement of funds by employees. It was then placed under administration in 2018 and its board was dissolved, leading to several investigations. It was in February this year, that NSFAS’ dismal state of affairs became apparent when an Auditor General’s report, released to the parliamentary portfolio committee on higher education, showed that the scheme had a complete lack of internal controls. Corruption Watch’s Kirsten Pearson had a front row seat…

They not been covering themselves in glory at all. It's quite a dysfunctional picture that emerges.

IS THE 3RD YEAR IN A ROW THAT THEY’VE RECEIVED A QUALIFIED AUDIT – AND THE LATEST WAS LITERALLY CALLED THE “WORST EVER” AS AN ASTOUNDING 7.5 BILLION RANDS WORTH OF IRREGULAR EXPENDITURE FROM PREVIOUS FINANCIAL YEARS HAS NOW COME TO LIGHT.

What irregular expenditure is, is it when the bookkeeping isn't quite in order for the process to authorize that use of funds wasn't done according to legislative prescript. So it is serious, but it doesn't mean that it didn't all reach students. The auditor general now has a new category called a material irregularity, and that is where the money has gone towards fraud and corruption at this stage they’re still figuring that out.

it's quite clear that the internal controls were not up to scratch, that IT systems were not sufficient to prevent this fraud syndicates from engaging in the corruption that they did.

Its maladministration made NSFAS a soft target for corrupt activities - leading to nearly half a million student records being irregular.

ANOTHER FINDING IN THE AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT IS THAT ONLY 40% OF THE 440,000 IRREGULAR RECORDS HAVE BEEN CHECKED – SO THEY WEREN’T EVEN CHECKING IF THE SUPPOSED STUDENT WAS REAL.

The report says there were a number of ‘ghost students” - these are students who don’t exist, yet are still being paid. What’s more, over half of the irregular student records haven’t even been investigated yet.

Claire: How prevalent are ghost students in the NSFAS system?

They don't give a number of ghost students. But they do mention that this fraud syndicates and essentially money being paid to people who are not students. And for me, that really gets me because that's the cost of corruption, where a genuine student that the kind of students that are writing to us saying we need a higher allowance, we kind of desperate, please, can you intervene in some way? Could be getting funding.

The myriad of forensic investigations have cost taxpayers R7 million: on the plus side, they’re helping root out the corruption at NSFAS, but they come at the cost of funding real students.

THERE ARE THOSE WHO USE THE STUDENTS’ PLIGHT FOR POLITICAL MILEAGE, AND THAT MAKES US FORGET WHO SHOULD BE HELD ACCOUNTABLE - IT PERPETUATES A MISTRUST OF UNIVERSITIES AS WELL AS LACK OF UNDERSTANDING OF WHAT HAPPENED.

Then you have our minister of higher education, Dr Blade Nzimande who says that what's happening at universities is like a soap opera. clearly the leadership is not up to the task.

In December, a new board was appointed at NSFAS, including a new CEO. We approached minister Nzimande but were told NSFAS spokesperson Kagisho Mamabolo would respond on government's behalf.

C: So you received three qualified audits the latest Being dubbed the worst ever? (clarify)

It's a it's a very big task for both the board and both the new CEO. The board and the CEO are working very hard to firstly support the institutions to ensure they help us to comply. Secondly is to make sure the I.T. system is fit for purpose.

To avoid potential corruption, NSFAS’ new system now uses a student’s South African ID to check that he or she actually exists and to verify the family’s financial status.

Another issue is that past student loans are not being repaid by the recipients, whether they’ve graduated or dropped out.

So before 2018, feel free education. Students understood that to be funded by NSFAS as a loan. You have to pay it back But since 2018, everyone gets a bursary. What does that mean? It means that you would have students that will drop out without even worrying About that money. we use the money we recover from our debtors to. To actually pay for future students, so it's in the interest of NSFAS beneficiary to pay their loan.

IT MAY NOT SOUND SEXY - BUT...SOCIAL JUSTICE CAN LOOK LIKE A LOT LIKE SIMPLE ADMINISTRATIVE JUSTICE

When you get the protests, it's the product of in this month and this month and this month and on this every single day, certain officials aren't showing up and doing the things that they need to be doing in their daily work to change that picture.

C: This is a weak point in our system?

One of the greatest things that happened under the NSFAS administration was to unravel coordinated fraud in some elements of syndicates that involve NSFAS officials, so what we have done to counter that is that we have opened a fraud line.

And the new board has referred a number of criminal complaints to the Special Investigating Unit. NSFAS suggests one reason the AG reports found ‘ghost students’ is because there is no check if a student has dropped out.

Are you paying people that are not even students or people who are somehow still receiving NSFAS funds?

Should a student exit the system. Without following the proper exit processes NSFAS will only pick them up in the subsequent year.

So there are some people who are receiving moneys.. Or Received money from the NSFAS and who are actually no longer students?

We don't pay ghost students, but we do pay or we could be paying for students who have bunked classes. We unfortunately, we cannot recover the allowances. It's lost, however, we can recover tuition.

ALMOST A THIRD OF SOUTH AFRICANS ARE COUNTED AS YOUTH…SO MONEY MISMANAGED THAT WAS MEANT TO EMPOWER THEM, CAN PROFOUNDLY HAMPER SOUTH AFRICA’S FUTURE.

NSFAS says it isn’t in control of the money once it's dispersed, but now has better internal controls to manage the funds.

We can't we can't dictate how should university run their disbursement system? That's why there's always a delay in January. That's why students always say I'm waiting for NSFAS. NSFAS has not paid. We can’t pay until the registration closes.

C: it sounds like it can change the trajectory of somebody's life if that education is interrupted for any reason. It's even more heartbreaking when you know that it is related to fraudulent activities or corruption or embezzlement or anything that Is 100 percent preventable?

KP: yeah, the course of someone's life and their ability to make a contribution can be altered when you don't get to complete your education and imagine having that grabbed away from you.

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 19 August 2021 Press Release: NSFAS in Shambles When former president Jacob Zuma said education would be free for students from low-income families, no one knew where the money would come from – the National Student Financial Aid Scheme (NSFAS) would have to overcome that challenge. Now, six years later, what little funds were found have been mismanaged because of a lack of accountability and management systems. This has led to R7-billion worth of irregular expenditure, corruption allegations and several investigations with the latest finding showing some funds have gone to "ghost students". As NSFAS counts the cost of its third bad audit outcome in a row, Carte Blanche investigates what it means for students who suffer the consequences when bursaries come late – or never. Producer: Sasha Schwendenwein | Presenter: Claire Mawisa Script: IT’S ALMOST BECOME AN ANNUAL RITUAL FOR STUDENTS TO PROTEST FOR THE RIGHT TO EDUCATION …AND FOR THE PROTEST TO BE MET WITH POLICE BRUTALITY AND VIOLENCE. BUT HERE’S WHAT BEING BROKE MEANS: POOR STUDENTS WHO CANNOT AFFORD TO BETTER THEMSELVES VERSUS AN EDUCATION SYSTEM THAT SAYS WE CANNOT AFFORD TO MAKE IT FREE. BUT WHAT NO ONE IS ASKING: IS GOVERNMENT MANAGING WHAT LITTLE FUNDS WE HAVE CORRECTLY? In 2015 Wits student Shaeera Kalla was shot 13 times with rubber bullets… but it’s 2021 and the FeesMustFall protests have continued as a symptom of the institutional failings of our government to fund its free education promise through the National Student Financial Aid Scheme or NSFAS. Shaeera: when the free education announcement was made by President Jacob Zuma, there was no indication of where the money was coming from. Kalla, a former student activist, feels the government hasn't found a solution to that conundrum. C: So then how does it feel for you personally when you see that the student protests are happening in 2021 for I could say exactly the same reasons? It's a very frustrating and disillusioning, you're not seeing any real change in these systems. NSFAS was still being seen as part of the solution, when in fact it was part of the problem. NSFAS falls under the department of higher education and training, and has existed since 1999, primarily offering student loans. But in 2015, it underwent a facelift almost overnight; and now it is 100% focused on giving bursaries. These NSFAS marketing videos explain what a student can now expect… Upsound: we get XYZ All a student needs in order to apply is a university acceptance and an annual household income less than R350,000. C: Has that not helped students? K: Fundamentally, we cannot say that NSFAS has become a competent institution that can administer the funds that have been put into it. Over the past 6 years NSFAS has been rocked by allegations of corruption and embezzlement of funds by employees. It was then placed under administration in 2018 and its board was dissolved, leading to several investigations. It was in February this year, that NSFAS’ dismal state of affairs became apparent when an Auditor General’s report, released to the parliamentary portfolio committee on higher education, showed that the scheme had a complete lack of internal controls. Corruption Watch’s Kirsten Pearson had a front row seat… They not been covering themselves in glory at all. It's quite a dysfunctional picture that emerges. IS THE 3RD YEAR IN A ROW THAT THEY’VE RECEIVED A QUALIFIED AUDIT – AND THE LATEST WAS LITERALLY CALLED THE “WORST EVER” AS AN ASTOUNDING 7.5 BILLION RANDS WORTH OF IRREGULAR EXPENDITURE FROM PREVIOUS FINANCIAL YEARS HAS NOW COME TO LIGHT. What irregular expenditure is, is it when the bookkeeping isn't quite in order for the process to authorize that use of funds wasn't done according to legislative prescript. So it is serious, but it doesn't mean that it didn't all reach students. The auditor general now has a new category called a material irregularity, and that is where the money has gone towards fraud and corruption at this stage they’re still figuring that out. it's quite clear that the internal controls were not up to scratch, that IT systems were not sufficient to prevent this fraud syndicates from engaging in the corruption that they did. Its maladministration made NSFAS a soft target for corrupt activities - leading to nearly half a million student records being irregular. ANOTHER FINDING IN THE AUDITOR GENERAL'S REPORT IS THAT ONLY 40% OF THE 440,000 IRREGULAR RECORDS HAVE BEEN CHECKED – SO THEY WEREN’T EVEN CHECKING IF THE SUPPOSED STUDENT WAS REAL. The report says there were a number of ‘ghost students” - these are students who don’t exist, yet are still being paid. What’s more, over half of the irregular student records haven’t even been investigated yet. Claire: How prevalent are ghost students in the NSFAS system? They don't give a number of ghost students. But they do mention that this fraud syndicates and essentially money being paid to people who are not students. And for me, that really gets me because that's the cost of corruption, where a genuine student that the kind of students that are writing to us saying we need a higher allowance, we kind of desperate, please, can you intervene in some way? Could be getting funding. The myriad of forensic investigations have cost taxpayers R7 million: on the plus side, they’re helping root out the corruption at NSFAS, but they come at the cost of funding real students. THERE ARE THOSE WHO USE THE STUDENTS’ PLIGHT FOR POLITICAL MILEAGE, AND THAT MAKES US FORGET WHO SHOULD BE HELD ACCOUNTABLE - IT PERPETUATES A MISTRUST OF UNIVERSITIES AS WELL AS LACK OF UNDERSTANDING OF WHAT HAPPENED. Then you have our minister of higher education, Dr Blade Nzimande who says that what's happening at universities is like a soap opera. clearly the leadership is not up to the task. In December, a new board was appointed at NSFAS, including a new CEO. We approached minister Nzimande but were told NSFAS spokesperson Kagisho Mamabolo would respond on government's behalf. C: So you received three qualified audits the latest Being dubbed the worst ever? (clarify) It's a it's a very big task for both the board and both the new CEO. The board and the CEO are working very hard to firstly support the institutions to ensure they help us to comply. Secondly is to make sure the I.T. system is fit for purpose. To avoid potential corruption, NSFAS’ new system now uses a student’s South African ID to check that he or she actually exists and to verify the family’s financial status. Another issue is that past student loans are not being repaid by the recipients, whether they’ve graduated or dropped out. So before 2018, feel free education. Students understood that to be funded by NSFAS as a loan. You have to pay it back But since 2018, everyone gets a bursary. What does that mean? It means that you would have students that will drop out without even worrying About that money. we use the money we recover from our debtors to. To actually pay for future students, so it's in the interest of NSFAS beneficiary to pay their loan. IT MAY NOT SOUND SEXY - BUT...SOCIAL JUSTICE CAN LOOK LIKE A LOT LIKE SIMPLE ADMINISTRATIVE JUSTICE When you get the protests, it's the product of in this month and this month and this month and on this every single day, certain officials aren't showing up and doing the things that they need to be doing in their daily work to change that picture. C: This is a weak point in our system? One of the greatest things that happened under the NSFAS administration was to unravel coordinated fraud in some elements of syndicates that involve NSFAS officials, so what we have done to counter that is that we have opened a fraud line. And the new board has referred a number of criminal complaints to the Special Investigating Unit. NSFAS suggests one reason the AG reports found ‘ghost students’ is because there is no check if a student has dropped out. Are you paying people that are not even students or people who are somehow still receiving NSFAS funds? Should a student exit the system. Without following the proper exit processes NSFAS will only pick them up in the subsequent year. So there are some people who are receiving moneys.. Or Received money from the NSFAS and who are actually no longer students? We don't pay ghost students, but we do pay or we could be paying for students who have bunked classes. We unfortunately, we cannot recover the allowances. It's lost, however, we can recover tuition. ALMOST A THIRD OF SOUTH AFRICANS ARE COUNTED AS YOUTH…SO MONEY MISMANAGED THAT WAS MEANT TO EMPOWER THEM, CAN PROFOUNDLY HAMPER SOUTH AFRICA’S FUTURE. NSFAS says it isn’t in control of the money once it's dispersed, but now has better internal controls to manage the funds. We can't we can't dictate how should university run their disbursement system? That's why there's always a delay in January. That's why students always say I'm waiting for NSFAS. NSFAS has not paid. We can’t pay until the registration closes. C: it sounds like it can change the trajectory of somebody's life if that education is interrupted for any reason. It's even more heartbreaking when you know that it is related to fraudulent activities or corruption or embezzlement or anything that Is 100 percent preventable? KP: yeah, the course of someone's life and their ability to make a contribution can be altered when you don't get to complete your education and imagine having that grabbed away from you.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): While everyone is looking at what's happening in the student protests, we should also be looking at NSFAS - because a closer look reveals R7 billion in irregular expenditure.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Parliament’s portfolio committee on Higher Education, Science and Technology has described the National Students Financial Aid Scheme (NSFAS) audit outcomes under administration as the “worst ever”. The latest NSFAS annual report has revealed irregular expenditure of R7.5 billion. Irregular expenditure is actually even higher, with the Auditor General saying that an additional R50bn in irregular expenditure 'should have been disclosed as a result of disbursements made against eligibility criteria and conditions that were set without consultations with the minister or eligibility criteria and conditions not gazetted'. Part of the problem that has given rise to the irregular expenditure is that there has been syndicated fraud and corruption where "ghost students" have been getting paid without proper checks being done before payments are made. Irregular expenditure is not corruption per se - it means that the proper procedures required by legislation have not been followed. The extent of corruption will be quantified when the amount lost due to 'material irregularity' - the Auditor General's new audit category that gives the AG teeth - is determined. However at the time of the audit, the amount lost due to material irregularity had not been determined by the NSFAS administrator, Randall Carolissen. It is clear that since his arrival as Administrator there are some new controls that have been put in place and cases of fraud have been handed over to law enforcement, whereas previously the irregular expenditure wasn't even being detected.
metadata.Summary: NSFAS has R7.5 billion in irregular expenditure. There is a further R50bn that the auditor general is concerned is irregular expenditure. This is the third year in a row that NSFAS has a qualified audit (bad audit outcome). Student protests come at the end of a chain of administrative actions that do not get performed timeously. In essence the Fees Must Fall protests are budget advocacy and a financial issue. If one reverses from the moment of Mthokozisi Ntumba's incredibly sad death, there has been a slow violence in the institutional failings at NSFAS. It may not be immediately apparent that social justice can looks like administrative justice and everyday actions that public officials must take require exercising their mandate in alignment with the Constitution and the Public Finance Management Act. The institution and its systems have been under enormous additional pressure since the 2015 fee free tertiary education announcement, as it would have suddenly needed to do a lot more than previously. It has emerged that there has been syndicated fraud and corruption. One of the types of fraud that have been discovered is that there have been ghost students who have been paid, because NSFAS wasn't doing enough to ensure that the students who were approved were indeed eligible to receive the funding. There are thousands of records of this nature, where students were approved without the correct documentation and checks being done. Only 40% of these records had been checked by the time the latest audit report was completed. To eradicate this syndicated fraud requires proper IT systems, good internal controls, integrity by those in key positions at NSFAS. A number of criminal complaints have been referred to the Special Investigating Unit to investigate. Parliament's Standing Committee on Public Accounts is frustrated with the pace of addressing these issues at NSFAS.
